content_voiceover: This slide gives a more structural, three-dimensional view of the same four vitamin K-dependent enzyme complexes we just discussed, now depicted assembled directly on the phospholipid bilayer membrane. On the upper left, the extrinsic tenase complex shows tissue factor anchored in the membrane, with VIIa and its substrate X and IX sitting on top. On the upper right, the intrinsic tenase complex shows VIIIa, IXa, and substrate X assembled together. Below, the prothrombinase complex shows Va, Xa, and substrate II clustered on the membrane surface. And on the lower right, the protein C complex, sometimes called the protein Case, shows thrombomodulin, TM, anchoring thrombin, IIa, and protein C, C, together. What makes all four of these complexes vitamin K-dependent is that factors II, VII, IX, X, and protein C all require vitamin K for the gamma-carboxylation of their glutamic acid residues, which is what allows them to bind calcium and dock onto the phospholipid membrane in the first place. This is exactly why warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, disrupts all four of these complexes simultaneously, and it's a concept that comes up constantly on boards.
keypoints: All four complexes assemble on an anionic phospholipid membrane
Factors II, VII, IX, X, and protein C are vitamin K-dependent
Vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation needed for calcium and membrane binding
Warfarin disrupts all four complexes by blocking vitamin K-dependent carboxylation
keypoint_voiceover: Remember, vitamin K-dependent factors are II, VII, IX, X, plus protein C and protein S. Warfarin knocks out all of them at once because it blocks the carboxylation step, not any single factor.
